conversations.title: Which growth problem are we solving?
conversations.setting: The lesson's executive requests a growth strategy without specifying revenue, profit, or market entry as the priority.
turns: Strategy lead
When you ask for a growth strategy, is the priority revenue, profit, or entry into another market?
Executive sponsor
I haven't chosen among those. I was assuming the same strategy would deliver all three.
Strategy lead
They may involve different choices. Could we clarify the ambition before building a strategic thesis?
Executive sponsor
What would a precise diagnosis add beyond a list of attractive growth initiatives?
Strategy lead
It identifies the problem we're trying to solve, rather than assuming every opportunity addresses it.
Executive sponsor
Then our issue tree should separate those three possible objectives instead of merge them.
Strategy lead
Exactly. We can ask what evidence would make each objective a priority and what constraints apply.
Executive sponsor
Please bring those questions into the discussion without inventing a target or investment budget.
Strategy lead
I will. The immediate output is a clarified decision question, not a fully approved growth direction.
Executive sponsor
Good. Let's establish the objective before requesting initiatives that might answer the wrong question.

conversations.title: Retention or acquisition behind the revenue concern
conversations.setting: Separate fictional strategy diagnosis: customer acquisition is unchanged, repeat purchases have fallen, and leadership asks for more advertising. Causes are unconfirmed.
turns: Commercial director
Revenue needs attention. Could you build a strategy around increasing advertising immediately?
Strategy analyst
Before selecting a response, can we clarify the problem? Acquisition is unchanged, while repeat purchases have fallen.
Commercial director
So our diagnosis should examine retention rather than assume new-customer volume caused the weakness.
Strategy analyst
It should investigate repeat purchasing, yes, without claiming we already know why it declined.
Commercial director
Could the issue tree separate purchase frequency, customer loss, and changes in order value?
Strategy analyst
Yes. Those are questions to test, not confirmed causes supplied by the current figures.
Commercial director
What would you ask me to clarify about the ambition for this work?
Strategy analyst
Whether we are prioritizing restored repeat revenue, total revenue growth, or profitability, and over what horizon.
Commercial director
I'll define that objective before treating additional advertising as the strategic thesis.
Strategy analyst
Then we can assess interventions against the actual diagnosis rather than start with a favored solution.

conversations.title: A capacity symptom needs a bounded question
conversations.setting: Separate fictional strategy exercise: one service team has a six-week backlog, while capacity elsewhere in the company has not been assessed.
turns: Chief operating officer
One team has a six-week backlog. Should our strategy be to acquire another service company?
Strategy director
Could we first clarify whether the priority is reducing that backlog or expanding long-term capability?
Chief operating officer
I was treating them as the same problem, but the immediate concern is waiting work.
Strategy director
Then our diagnosis should examine demand, capacity, and work flow before selecting an acquisition response.
Chief operating officer
Do we know whether another internal team has spare capacity that could help?
Strategy director
No. Capacity elsewhere hasn't been assessed, so we shouldn't assume either spare resources or universal shortage.
Chief operating officer
Let's frame the issue around the affected service and the six-week backlog first.
Strategy director
Agreed. An issue tree can organize the questions without making the proposed acquisition the answer in advance.
Chief operating officer
I'll clarify the desired service outcome and any constraints for that investigation.
Strategy director
Then we'll assess strategic options after the problem and evidence are properly defined.

additional_scenario.title: Efficiency has two meanings
additional_scenario.brief: In a fictional executive discussion, finance means lower total cost by efficiency, while operations means shorter customer waiting time. No preferred objective or numeric target is agreed.
additional_scenario.role_a: You are the strategy facilitator. Clarify the two objectives and ask which decision the analysis should support.
additional_scenario.role_b: You sponsor the work. Explain why the objectives may require different evidence and remain unprioritized.
additional_scenario.opening_line: Could we distinguish lower total cost from shorter waiting time before calling this one efficiency objective?
additional_scenario.complication: A participant wants a target announced immediately without a baseline.
success_checks: Name both meanings accurately.
Keep the target and priority unagreed.
Agree a bounded objective-setting question before choosing initiatives.

conversations.title: Core improvement and market entry share the same people
conversations.setting: The lesson's team can invest in its core service or enter a new segment; staff capacity is limited and shared.
turns: Strategy manager
Both options use the same limited staff. We can't compare them as if each had a separate team.
Business sponsor
Could we call both priorities and ask people to deliver them alongside normal work?
Strategy manager
That avoids the tradeoff rather than resolves it. The opportunity cost is what those people cannot do instead.
Business sponsor
The core-service option strengthens existing work, whereas segment entry pursues a new customer group.
Strategy manager
Yes. We should compare the same staffing period, expected outcomes, and uncertainty for both.
Business sponsor
We haven't quantified those outcomes, so neither option has a proven higher return yet.
Strategy manager
Correct. The activity system also matters: which supporting work each choice would require.
Business sponsor
I'll ask both proposal owners to identify displaced work instead of hiding the resource conflict.
Strategy manager
Then we can present a real strategic choice with common criteria and its weaker side visible.
Business sponsor
Good. Our next discussion will prioritize, not simply add two labels to an overloaded team.

conversations.title: A focused pilot or a wider launch
conversations.setting: Separate fictional strategy exercise: with the same six-person team for a quarter, option A serves one segment and includes research; B serves three segments but has no research capacity.
turns: Growth director
Option B reaches three segments, so it looks stronger than the one-segment pilot.
Strategy analyst
Both use six people for the quarter, but only A includes capacity for customer research.
Growth director
Then the tradeoff is broader initial coverage versus more deliberate learning in one segment.
Strategy analyst
Exactly. More segments doesn't itself prove more profitable growth, especially with their needs still untested.
Growth director
Could we keep B's reach and add A's research without changing the team?
Strategy analyst
Not under these supplied options. We'd need to reassess scope rather than assume extra capacity.
Growth director
I favor learning first, but want the lost early coverage stated as the opportunity cost.
Strategy analyst
I'll make that explicit and retain the same quarterly staffing basis for the comparison.
Growth director
Then the recommendation can explain a strategic choice instead of calling one option best at everything.
Strategy analyst
Agreed. We can propose A for review while keeping its narrower reach visible.

conversations.title: Customization versus a repeatable service
conversations.setting: Separate fictional strategy workshop: option A offers bespoke implementations with more configuration work; B standardizes the service but excludes some requested custom features. Revenue effects are unknown.
turns: Product director
The bespoke option answers more individual requests. Should we call it the obvious way to win?
Operations strategist
It also requires more configuration work, whereas the standardized option excludes some custom features.
Product director
So we should compare customer fit and delivery effort rather than count features alone.
Operations strategist
Yes. Those choices imply different activity systems, not just different descriptions of the same offer.
Product director
Do we know whether broader customization produces enough revenue to justify that work?
Operations strategist
No. Revenue effects are unknown here, so neither margin advantage is established.
Product director
I'll describe the opportunity cost of standardization as requests we deliberately don't support.
Operations strategist
And describe the bespoke option's tradeoff as additional configuration work rather than free flexibility.
Product director
Let's assess both over the same customer scope and planning horizon before recommending one.
Operations strategist
Good. A useful strategic choice states what we give up as clearly as what we pursue.

additional_scenario.title: Support hours or development capacity
additional_scenario.brief: A fictional team can allocate two specialists for the next quarter either to longer support hours or to a product improvement project. Existing hours and project scope would otherwise remain unchanged.
additional_scenario.role_a: You are the strategy analyst. Compare the alternatives on the same staffing period.
additional_scenario.role_b: You sponsor the decision. State a preferred benefit and acknowledge the work forgone.
additional_scenario.opening_line: The same two specialists can extend support or work on the improvement project, so choosing one displaces the other.
additional_scenario.complication: A stakeholder asks you to announce both outcomes without additional resources.
success_checks: Keep the two-specialist quarterly constraint explicit.
State the benefit and opportunity cost of each option.
Offer a reviewable priority rather than promise both.

conversations.title: Industry spending exceeds the serviceable segment
conversations.setting: The lesson's market estimate uses total industry spending, but the company can serve only one customer segment.
turns: Strategy analyst
The estimate uses total industry spending, while our current offer can serve only one customer segment.
Executive sponsor
Can we present that total as the market we can realistically capture?
Strategy analyst
No. Total addressable market and our serviceable market need to be distinguished before discussing obtainable share.
Executive sponsor
So TAM, SAM, and SOM shouldn't all carry the same number by default.
Strategy analyst
Correct. We haven't established the relevant segment size or a defensible obtainable share here.
Executive sponsor
Could a large industry total still tell us where the profit pool sits?
Strategy analyst
Not by itself. Spending volume doesn't identify where profits are earned within the industry.
Executive sponsor
I'll keep the industry context but remove the claim that all of it is serviceable.
Strategy analyst
I'll request segment evidence and clarify which assumptions would support an obtainable-market estimate.
Executive sponsor
Good. The opportunity statement should match our actual reach rather than a broad headline number.

conversations.title: A market-share aspiration is not a sales forecast
conversations.setting: Separate fictional sizing exercise: a serviceable market is estimated at $20 million, and a team proposes a 5% share target without acquisition evidence.
turns: Business development lead
Five percent of the twenty-million-dollar estimate is one million. Can we call that next year's sales forecast?
Strategy researcher
The arithmetic works, but the five-percent share is an aspiration without acquisition evidence.
Business development lead
Then the one-million-dollar figure is conditional on an unsupported share assumption.
Strategy researcher
Exactly. A serviceable market estimate doesn't establish an obtainable market or a timed revenue forecast.
Business development lead
What would make the SOM discussion more grounded than selecting a convenient percentage?
Strategy researcher
Evidence about reach, capacity, conversion, and relevant competition, with the assumptions stated explicitly.
Business development lead
We haven't supplied those inputs, so I'll present the share as a proposed target only.
Strategy researcher
Also preserve uncertainty in the twenty-million-dollar estimate rather than treat it as exact measured demand.
Business development lead
I'll separate market estimate, share ambition, and sales forecast in the meeting.
Strategy researcher
Good. That prevents correct multiplication from disguising an unsupported commercial conclusion.

conversations.title: More revenue does not locate the profit pool
conversations.setting: Separate fictional industry exercise: distribution has higher reported revenue than specialist servicing, but comparable cost data is unavailable.
turns: Strategy associate
Distribution reports more revenue than specialist servicing. Is that where the largest profit pool must be?
Strategy director
Not necessarily. Revenue and profit differ, and comparable cost data isn't available here.
Strategy associate
So industry scale doesn't by itself establish where value is retained after costs.
Strategy director
Correct. We also need comparable business boundaries before interpreting the two reported figures.
Strategy associate
Could we assume servicing has higher margins because it sounds more specialized?
Strategy director
No. That would substitute a plausible story for evidence about actual economics.
Strategy associate
I'll describe the observed revenue difference and identify profitability as an open question.
Strategy director
Good. Our market-entry discussion should not treat an unmeasured profit pool as confirmed.
Strategy associate
I'll seek comparable cost and scope information before recommending where to compete.
Strategy director
Then the analysis can distinguish industry structure evidence from assumptions about attractive returns.

additional_scenario.title: Global spending with a regional offer
additional_scenario.brief: A fictional market slide uses a global spending estimate, but the company's current service is available in one region. That region's share of spending is unmeasured.
additional_scenario.role_a: You review the sizing. Explain the gap between global context and current serviceability.
additional_scenario.role_b: You prepared the slide. Identify the regional evidence needed without inventing a share.
additional_scenario.opening_line: The global figure provides context, but it doesn't establish the market our current regional offer can serve.
additional_scenario.complication: A sponsor suggests dividing the global estimate equally among regions despite no supporting evidence.
success_checks: Distinguish global spending from current reach.
Reject an unsupported equal-share assumption.
Agree a regional evidence request and qualified sizing statement.

conversations.title: Growth with negative contribution
conversations.setting: The lesson's new service has rising revenue but negative contribution after variable delivery costs; a slide calls growth proof of a sound model.
turns: Business unit director
Revenue is growing. Why can't we call that proof of a sound business model?
Strategy finance lead
The service has negative contribution after variable delivery costs, so growth alone doesn't establish sound economics.
Business unit director
Could you explain contribution in terms the operating team will recognize?
Strategy finance lead
Here, it's revenue minus those variable delivery costs, before considering the other costs not included.
Business unit director
So more sales can coexist with an unfavorable contribution, rather than automatically create margin expansion.
Strategy finance lead
Exactly. We need to understand the value drivers and costs before claiming profitable scaling.
Business unit director
Does negative contribution alone settle our long-term right to win in the market?
Strategy finance lead
No. That broader capability question also needs evidence; neither conclusion follows from revenue growth alone.
Business unit director
I'll separate demand growth from the unresolved economic and capability questions.
Strategy finance lead
Good. The slide should explain what improved and what still undermines the model.

conversations.title: A contribution calculation before fixed costs
conversations.setting: Separate fictional service example: each job earns $80 and incurs $50 variable delivery cost; fixed overhead and invested capital are not supplied.
turns: Service director
Each job earns eighty dollars and costs fifty in variable delivery. Is thirty dollars our final profit?
Strategy analyst
It is contribution per job in this example, not final profit after all costs.
Service director
Because fixed overhead hasn't been deducted from that thirty-dollar difference.
Strategy analyst
Correct. And we haven't supplied invested capital, so this doesn't establish return on invested capital, or ROIC.
Service director
Then a useful value driver might be delivery efficiency, but we still need evidence about feasible improvements.
Strategy analyst
Exactly. A smaller variable cost would change contribution in the model, not prove an improvement has occurred.
Service director
I'll explain the eighty-minus-fifty calculation and keep the missing overhead visible.
Strategy analyst
Good. That lets colleagues understand unit economics without mistaking one layer for complete profitability.
Service director
We'll discuss margin expansion only with the relevant cost basis and assumptions clear.
Strategy analyst
Agreed. The simple calculation should illuminate the model, not conceal its incomplete inputs.

conversations.title: Owning data is not yet a right to win
conversations.setting: Separate fictional strategy review: a company owns a historical service dataset but has not tested its usefulness for a proposed analytics product.
turns: Product strategist
We own the historical dataset. Doesn't that give us a right to win in analytics?
Strategy director
It may be an asset, but we haven't tested its usefulness for the proposed customer problem.
Product strategist
So a resource is something we possess, while a capability is what we can reliably do with it.
Strategy director
Exactly. Advantage also depends on whether that capability creates relevant value compared with alternatives.
Product strategist
Could we call the dataset a proven value driver before customers use the proposed product?
Strategy director
Not on this evidence. Its relevance and practical usefulness remain hypotheses to assess.
Product strategist
I'll describe the dataset as a potential input, not proof of a defensible business model.
Strategy director
Good. Also identify any usage constraints before assuming every record is available for the new purpose.
Product strategist
We'll test usefulness and clarify constraints before presenting a right-to-win claim.
Strategy director
That distinguishes a promising resource from demonstrated capability and competitive advantage.

additional_scenario.title: Automation savings exclude support work
additional_scenario.brief: A fictional service model shows ten minutes less manual processing per job, but any additional support work has not been measured. A slide claims total delivery cost fell.
additional_scenario.role_a: You explain unit economics. Separate observed processing time from full delivery cost.
additional_scenario.role_b: You own operations. Ask what support and cost evidence is needed to assess margin improvement.
additional_scenario.opening_line: Processing takes ten fewer minutes, but total delivery cost hasn't been established without the support work.
additional_scenario.complication: A colleague wants to call the time difference a verified profit increase.
success_checks: Preserve the ten-minute observation.
Distinguish task time, delivery cost, and profit.
Agree to measure missing work before claiming margin expansion.

conversations.title: Two investment requests need displaced-work choices
conversations.setting: The lesson's two divisions request the same investment budget; neither explains what work would stop if funded.
turns: Portfolio director
Both divisions request the same investment budget. What would each stop or defer if it were funded?
Division sponsor
Neither proposal identifies displaced work. We presented them as additions to the current portfolio.
Portfolio director
Then capital allocation isn't fully described. The resource tradeoff needs to be explicit.
Division sponsor
Could we approve the preferred proposal first and decide what to stop later?
Portfolio director
We can take it for review, but shouldn't promise resources without examining the competing commitments.
Division sponsor
I'll ask each division for a funded option and the work it would defer.
Portfolio director
Good. Distinguish protecting the core business from exploring an adjacency, without assuming one always wins.
Division sponsor
We'll also identify approvals required before either option becomes a commitment.
Portfolio director
Then we can negotiate scope or sequencing with the consequences visible.
Division sponsor
Agreed. The next review will contain choices, not two requests that both assume the full budget.

conversations.title: Funding a pilot by deferring a rollout
conversations.setting: Separate fictional portfolio exercise: a team has a fixed $100,000 budget. A $20,000 adjacency pilot could be funded only by reducing a planned $100,000 core rollout to $80,000; approval is pending.
turns: Innovation sponsor
Could we fund the twenty-thousand-dollar adjacency pilot within the existing hundred-thousand-dollar budget?
Portfolio manager
Only by reducing the planned core rollout to eighty thousand under this proposal.
Innovation sponsor
Then my offer is a smaller pilot funded through a defined reduction, not extra money.
Portfolio manager
Yes. What core rollout work would the twenty-thousand-dollar reduction actually defer?
Innovation sponsor
That scope hasn't been identified yet, so I can't claim the core business is unaffected.
Portfolio manager
Please obtain that detail before we ask for approval of the capital allocation.
Innovation sponsor
If the reduced rollout is acceptable, can we take both linked scopes for review?
Portfolio manager
Yes, as a conditional proposal. I can't confirm approval or resource release today.
Innovation sponsor
I'll keep the two budgets together and show the deferred work once assessed.
Portfolio manager
Good. The funding conversation will expose the tradeoff instead of presenting the pilot as free.

conversations.title: A divestiture idea cannot fund spending yet
conversations.setting: Separate fictional portfolio review: a team proposes selling a noncore unit to fund investment, but no buyer, valuation, or sale timing is confirmed.
turns: Business sponsor
Could we commit the new investment now and pay for it from the planned divestiture?
Capital allocation lead
The sale is only a proposal. Buyer, value, and timing are all unconfirmed.
Business sponsor
Then what can we offer the investment team without promising unavailable proceeds?
Capital allocation lead
We can assess a staged proposal with funding conditions explicit, rather than authorize the full spend.
Business sponsor
Would the first stage also need its own identified funding and approval?
Capital allocation lead
Yes. Calling a stage small doesn't create budget or remove the decision requirement.
Business sponsor
I'll request a bounded scope and distinguish its funding from the hypothetical sale.
Capital allocation lead
Good. Keep the noncore-unit review separate from any conclusion that divestiture is already agreed.
Business sponsor
Then our recommendation can present the dependency and alternative sequencing for decision.
Capital allocation lead
Exactly. Negotiate what can be assessed now without converting a possible transaction into cash on hand.

additional_scenario.title: Shared specialists block two funded projects
additional_scenario.brief: Two fictional portfolio projects each have budget approval, but both require the same specialist during the same month. Only one month's specialist capacity is available; project sequencing is undecided.
additional_scenario.role_a: You manage the portfolio. Explain why funding approval doesn't resolve the staffing conflict.
additional_scenario.role_b: You sponsor one project. Offer a sequencing proposal and state what would be delayed.
additional_scenario.opening_line: Both budgets are approved, but the shared specialist cannot cover both projects in the same month.
additional_scenario.complication: A sponsor asks you to confirm parallel delivery because the money is already allocated.
success_checks: Separate budget from specialist capacity.
Offer a concrete sequencing tradeoff.
Keep the changed delivery commitments subject to review.

conversations.title: Possible synergies without an integration estimate
conversations.setting: The lesson's acquisition proposal lists possible cost savings but has no integration plan or implementation estimate.
turns: Acquisition sponsor
The proposal lists cost savings. Can we present them as the acquisition's confirmed value creation?
Strategy lead
No. They are possible synergies, and we lack an integration plan and implementation estimate.
Acquisition sponsor
Then gross savings and net benefit are different claims in this discussion.
Strategy lead
Exactly. Post-merger integration, or PMI, may require costs and work that aren't estimated here.
Acquisition sponsor
Could we assume integration is straightforward because the businesses look similar?
Strategy lead
Similarity isn't evidence that systems, roles, and operating processes will combine easily.
Acquisition sponsor
I'll label the savings as proposed and identify the missing implementation work.
Strategy lead
Good. The build-buy-partner comparison should include realistic execution assumptions for each route.
Acquisition sponsor
We'll seek integration input before treating the acquisition as the proven best growth option.
Strategy lead
Then leadership can distinguish strategic logic from benefits that still need validation and delivery.

conversations.title: A partnership discussion is not secured market access
conversations.setting: Separate fictional market-entry exercise: a potential distributor has expressed interest, but no agreement, coverage commitment, or commercial terms are established.
turns: Market entry director
The distributor is interested. Can the strategy update say we've secured access to the market?
Partnerships lead
Not yet. Interest isn't an agreement, and coverage commitments and commercial terms remain open.
Market entry director
Then the partner route is a potential option, not a completed market-entry capability.
Partnerships lead
Correct. We should also assess what the distributor can actually deliver rather than infer reach from enthusiasm.
Market entry director
Could we include projected sales as guaranteed because a channel conversation is underway?
Partnerships lead
No. That would add certainty unsupported by either the relationship or demand evidence.
Market entry director
I'll report the discussion milestone and the unresolved commercial questions separately.
Partnerships lead
Good. We can compare build, buy, and partner routes without calling the partner route secured.
Market entry director
Please bring the next evidence needed for a credible coverage assessment.
Partnerships lead
I will, with any scenario assumptions clearly separated from confirmed commitments.

conversations.title: Overlapping teams do not prove removable costs
conversations.setting: Separate fictional acquisition exercise: both firms have customer-support teams, but workload, service requirements, and integration costs have not been assessed.
turns: Deal analyst
Both firms have support teams. Can we count one team's cost as an automatic synergy?
Integration manager
No. Overlapping job labels don't show that the combined workload can be handled by one team.
Deal analyst
So the observation is duplication of functions, not confirmed removable capacity.
Integration manager
Exactly. We need workload, service requirements, and implementation costs before estimating a defensible net benefit.
Deal analyst
Would using a standard percentage reduction make the estimate more credible?
Integration manager
Only if it has relevant support. A convenient percentage doesn't replace an integration assessment.
Deal analyst
I'll describe a potential support-efficiency opportunity and keep the savings amount unestablished.
Integration manager
Good. PMI planning also needs to consider service continuity rather than treat every overlap as unnecessary.
Deal analyst
We'll request the operational evidence before including a firm saving in the acquisition case.
Integration manager
Then the synergy discussion can move from a plausible idea to an assessed proposal.

additional_scenario.title: A build estimate excludes customer support
additional_scenario.brief: A fictional build-buy-partner comparison prices the build option's software development but omits ongoing customer support. The other options include support estimates. No preferred route is approved.
additional_scenario.role_a: You review the strategy case. Identify the scope mismatch and limit the cost conclusion.
additional_scenario.role_b: You own the build proposal. Ask for support requirements and retain the estimate as partial.
additional_scenario.opening_line: The build figure excludes customer support, so it isn't yet comparable with the other two estimates.
additional_scenario.complication: A sponsor wants to call building the cheapest route before the missing work is costed.
success_checks: Identify the omitted support scope.
Keep the build total and route preference unconfirmed.
Agree a consistent-scope assessment before ranking options.

conversations.title: Comparing scenarios without naming a prediction
conversations.setting: Separate fictional quarterly planning exercise: option A reserves capacity for 100 jobs at a total quarterly cost of $10,000; B reserves 60 jobs for $6,000. Both cover the same service and quarter. Base-case demand is 90 jobs; downside demand is 50. Demand figures are assumptions, and revenue is unestimated.
turns: Planning sponsor
The base case assumes ninety jobs this quarter; the downside assumes fifty. Which is our prediction?
Strategy facilitator
Neither is established as a prediction. Let's compare both capacity options under those assumptions.
Planning sponsor
A provides one hundred slots for ten thousand dollars, while B provides sixty for six thousand.
Strategy facilitator
In the base case, A covers ninety jobs; B leaves thirty beyond its reserved capacity.
Planning sponsor
In the downside case, both cover fifty, but A has fifty unused slots and B ten.
Strategy facilitator
Correct. A costs four thousand more for the same quarter but accommodates higher demand.
Planning sponsor
So B limits committed cost, whereas A provides more capacity if the base case occurs.
Strategy facilitator
Yes. Revenue is unestimated, so this comparison doesn't establish which option would be more profitable.
Planning sponsor
Let's take that cost-capacity tradeoff for review instead of calling either scenario certain.
Strategy facilitator
Agreed. We'll retain both demand assumptions and the residual uncertainty in the recommendation.

conversations.title: A short lease preserves flexibility at a higher cost
conversations.setting: Separate fictional strategy exercise: a one-year facility option costs more annually but preserves an earlier exit; a three-year option costs less annually but commits longer. Other terms are unassessed.
turns: Operations director
The three-year option is cheaper annually. Should we choose it under both demand scenarios?
Strategy analyst
It also commits us longer, whereas the one-year option costs more but preserves an earlier exit.
Operations director
Then the strategic option we're comparing includes flexibility, not simply annual price.
Strategy analyst
Exactly. Under uncertain demand, the ability to reconsider earlier may matter, but its value isn't quantified here.
Operations director
Could we say the short option is always safer without checking the other terms?
Strategy analyst
No. Other terms remain unassessed, and different scenarios may make the tradeoff look different.
Operations director
I'll compare annual cost and commitment length consistently, with demand assumptions stated.
Strategy analyst
Good. Don't compare one year's total with three years' total as though the periods match.
Operations director
We'll review the remaining terms before recommending how much flexibility to preserve.
Strategy analyst
Then the decision can acknowledge both the price advantage and the longer commitment it buys.

conversations.title: A review trigger is not an automatic expansion order
conversations.setting: Separate fictional plan: two consecutive months above a demand threshold trigger strategy review, not automatic expansion. Only one month qualifies. For the coming month, preparation-only would cost $2,000 for a capacity assessment and create no external contract; immediate expansion would cost $12,000 monthly under a six-month capacity contract. Neither option is approved.
turns: Commercial sponsor
Demand crossed the threshold once. Can we expand next month instead of only preparing?
Strategy manager
The trigger requires two consecutive months and initiates review, not automatic expansion. Neither option is approved.
Commercial sponsor
Compare the coming month's commitments so I can see what each option actually involves.
Strategy manager
Preparation costs two thousand dollars for an assessment; expansion costs twelve thousand for capacity next month.
Commercial sponsor
That's ten thousand more next month. Does expansion also commit us beyond that period?
Strategy manager
Yes, twelve thousand monthly for six months. Preparation creates no external contract, but adds no capacity.
Commercial sponsor
So preparation preserves flexibility, whereas expansion supplies capacity sooner with a longer financial commitment.
Strategy manager
Exactly. One qualifying month doesn't establish sustained demand or justify treating either option as authorized.
Commercial sponsor
I'll take preparation as my preferred proposal for review, with the capacity limitation explicit.
Strategy manager
I'll record that preference, not approval. The second demand month and any spending decision remain pending.

additional_scenario.title: A reversible pilot versus a permanent rollout
additional_scenario.brief: A fictional strategy team compares a three-month pilot that can be stopped at review with a permanent rollout requiring a longer commitment. Costs and customer outcomes are not yet estimated.
additional_scenario.role_a: You are the strategy analyst. Compare commitment and learning while preserving missing economic information.
additional_scenario.role_b: You sponsor the choice. Explain which flexibility matters and ask what would trigger further investment.
additional_scenario.opening_line: The pilot provides an earlier review point, whereas the rollout commits us longer; their costs remain unestimated.
additional_scenario.complication: A colleague wants to call the pilot risk-free because it can be stopped.
success_checks: State the three-month review point and longer rollout commitment.
Avoid claiming reversibility removes all risk or cost.
Agree evidence needed for the next investment decision.

conversations.title: Twelve metrics and one missing request
conversations.setting: Separate fictional extension of the lesson: a twelve-metric board presentation seeks approval for a four-week, twenty-account pilot. Operations estimates ten support hours weekly, but only six are available. Additional staffing and pilot approval are unconfirmed; the board holds approval authority.
turns: Strategy director
Our twelve metrics don't state the request. What decision are we asking the board to make?
Executive sponsor
Approval for a four-week pilot with twenty accounts, not a permanent rollout or immediate expansion.
Strategy director
Before presenting that request, operations, what constraint does the board need to hear?
Operations lead
The pilot needs ten support hours weekly, but we have six. Four hours remain uncovered.
Strategy director
So the proposed scope exceeds available support. Can we assume colleagues will absorb those four hours?
Operations lead
No. Additional staffing is unconfirmed. We should assess extra coverage or a smaller pilot scope.
Strategy director
That makes support capacity an unresolved condition. Sponsor, will you own presenting the conditional request?
Executive sponsor
Yes. I'll present the scope and coverage gap, with board approval explicitly pending.
Strategy director
Operations, please own the coverage-options assessment before that discussion. Can you confirm the handoff?
Operations lead
I accept that assessment. I'll return feasible options, not promise additional staffing; pilot approval remains pending.

conversations.title: A KPI owner is not automatically the decision owner
conversations.setting: Separate fictional pilot: conversion improved, and analytics owns reporting that KPI. The sponsor alone decides extension. A proposed fifty-client extension requires twenty support hours weekly; operations has twelve available. Additional coverage is unconfirmed, and extension is unapproved.
turns: Program manager
Conversion improved. Can analytics announce the proposed fifty-client extension, or is another decision needed?
Analytics lead
I own the KPI report, not extension approval. The sponsor holds that decision right.
Program manager
Operations, what would supporting fifty clients require, and what capacity do you actually have?
Operations lead
We need twenty support hours weekly and have twelve available. Eight hours remain uncovered.
Program manager
Then improved conversion doesn't resolve delivery capacity. Would a smaller scope or extra coverage need assessment?
Operations lead
Yes. Neither solution is confirmed, so we cannot promise support for fifty clients yet.
Program manager
Analytics, please provide the measured result without an approval claim. Can you own that part?
Analytics lead
Yes. I'll provide the KPI evidence and distinguish it from the sponsor's pending extension decision.
Program manager
Operations, will you own assessing coverage or reduced scope? We'll present that gap alongside the KPI.
Operations lead
I accept the assessment and will return the options. The fifty-client extension remains unapproved pending the sponsor's review.

conversations.title: A steering meeting ends with an unresolved owner
conversations.setting: Separate fictional execution review: commercial and operations teams each assume the other owns customer onboarding in a proposed service; no ownership decision has been made.
turns: Steering chair
Commercial and operations each expect the other to own onboarding. We need to resolve that operating-model question.
Program director
Could we list both teams as owners and move to the next agenda item?
Steering chair
Shared participation doesn't explain who is accountable for the decision and the actual handoff.
Program director
Then we should hear what each team can own before proposing an allocation.
Steering chair
Exactly. Invite both perspectives, including any capacity constraints we haven't assessed.
Program director
Who can confirm the final ownership arrangement after that discussion?
Steering chair
That decision right hasn't been established in this exercise. We need the sponsor to clarify it.
Program director
I'll record that as a specific action rather than infer agreement because nobody objected.
Steering chair
Good. Close with onboarding ownership unresolved and the sponsor clarification assigned to you.
Program director
I accept that action and won't describe the operating model as approved until the decision is confirmed.

additional_scenario.title: A board discussion praised the pilot but did not approve expansion
additional_scenario.brief: A fictional board discussion praised pilot learning but deferred the expansion decision until costs are reviewed. The draft internal update says expansion approved. Finance has not supplied the cost review.
additional_scenario.role_a: You facilitate the follow-up. Restate the actual decision and invite finance's missing input.
additional_scenario.role_b: You sponsor the pilot. Confirm the deferred decision and identify who will bring the cost review.
additional_scenario.opening_line: The board welcomed the learning but deferred expansion pending the cost review; approval has not been given.
additional_scenario.complication: A team lead wants to begin expansion because the feedback sounded positive.
success_checks: Separate positive discussion from approval.
Identify the pending finance input.
Close with accurate decision status and a named follow-up responsibility.
